text:
[25M] Planning first solo trip, thinking of bikepacking in Belgium and The Netherlands and looking for general advice
Hello! I (25M) am starting to think about my first solo trip. I traveled as a kid/teenager with family (a couple trips to Europe) and they were always densely planned - that is, we had a handful of activities booked a day and always felt like we were racing from point A to point B. For me, this felt kind of stressful, so I want to take a stab at a more relaxed/loose agenda for my first solo trip.

I'm currently planning the following, for a ~2 week trip (flexible on length, but don't wanna overdo it and burn out). I don't have any particular "goals" with this trip, other than getting away from my routine for a bit and getting some exercise along the way. One wrinkle is that I don't have a touring bike worth bringing, so I'm planning to just buy a solid used bike in Belgium and get it equipped (rack/pannier/frame bag), ideally under 600 euros. Part of the desire for flexibility on this trip stems from this part since it may take me 2-3 days to figure this part out, or it'll happen on day 1. Overall, I am *not* looking to cheap out, as a whole, on this trip. I don't spend much money on travel, so I'm not going to shy away from creature comforts (private hostel room, food, tours/museums that interest me).

* London (3-4 days)
  * Totally separate from the BE/NL legs of the trip, I spent some time in London a couple years ago and just want to spend a little time alone here. 
  * Hoping to experience some night life and relaxing days (museums, food, walking about). Open to any and all suggestions for finding lodging and activities.
* Ghent or Bruges (by train; 2-3 days)
  * Planning to find a used bike to buy here, and get it equipped as needed for the trip; will discard my existing luggage (planning to bring something cheap and junky)
* Ride to Middelburg (1 night)
  * Not much to do here as far as I know, just a stopping point. Might use Warmshowers or just a B&B.
  * Stop at the Delta Works/Oosterscheldekering on the way out (I'm an engineer, lol)
* Continue to Rotterdam (2-3 days)
  * IDRK much about Rotterdam/Hague so let me know what I should look out for / whether I should go somewhere else!
* Utrecht (2-3 days)
  * I'm told this is like a little Amsterdam with fewer tourists, so I'm interested in spending a bit of time here. Looking to enjoy a walking tour and some night life here, so hoping to stay in a more social hostel.
* Amsterdam (2-3 days)
  * Final stop; sell the bike at the very end, or give it away to a lucky local if I can't find a buyer in time (OR, I fall in love with the thing and figure out how to fly it home, lol).

I know this is a lot, and I probably sound kind of aimless (which makes it hard to give advice!) but I am all ears for any and all info you might have. Any towns I should skip, or make sure I check out on the way? Any activities you recommend or suggest I avoid? If you've got experience bikepacking (this is my first trip!), any thoughts? For a little background, I bike commute all over NYC and have comfortably been riding 25+ miles on weekends on a shitty old Hard Rock, so I'm not too concerned about my own ability to cover the ground. However, any tips on gear and equipment would be super helpful!
label: advice_seeking

text:
My First Solo Travel Experience: the highest of highs and lowest of lows
Trip Report
I recently moved to Dublin, Ireland from the USA. And while that has been an amazing, life changing experience in itself, that's not what this post is about.

I had always been intrigued by the idea of solo travel. The thought of having complete freedom of what I wanted to do sounded really appealing to me, and the amount of fear that would have to be overcome to do such a thing sounded like a great opportunity for personal growth.

The opportunity arose to visit Copenhagen, Denmark, over a long weekend in December. I didn't know anything about the country prior to choosing the country. As my first Christmas in Europe, I was looking for a place with high vaccination rates that would have great Christmas Markets to visit, and Copenhagen fit the bill.

The Bad

Both the time leading up to the trip and the beginning of the trip were very challenging for me.

Leading up to the trip, I was extremely nervous about covid, and the prospect of testing positive and getting stuck in the country.

When I landed in Copenhagen, I had no idea I'd have to go through customs, as I naively thought countries within the EU had no formal border crossings. Not a big deal, but it caught me off guard and ended with a panic attack in front of the customs agent. Not a great look!

That was nothing compared to the panic that followed. When I left the airport and took the metro to my AirBnB, I got lost. Also not a huge deal, except it was midnight, 2 degrees Celsius, and the signs I needed to use outside the apartment to find my AirBnB were all in Danish. Something about the combination of all of this happening in a foreign country made it feel like it wasn't real, or that I was in a bad dream.

The last bad dream of the night was the AirBnB itself. Don't get me wrong, the accommodations and host were great. But I had never stayed in an AirBnB where I am just renting a room and sharing an apartment before, so this was a big source of discomfort in the beginning as well. The host did a great job at making me feel at home thankfully, and this discomfort did not last long.

The Good

Fortunately, after a good night's sleep and the logistics of arriving being settled, the scary part of the trip was over. Now, it was time to explore Copenhagen!

I started the day just exploring outside the apartment. There is something about visiting a new country where the language is different than yours that makes you feel like you are on a different planet. I was also fascinated by all the little subtle differences, like how healthy the foods in the 7/11s were, or how it felt like there were more bikes than cars. I really took in all the sights, smells, and sounds of my surroundings in ways that I wouldn't have had I not been by myself.

After a bit of exploring I spent a good chunk of the afternoon at the National Museum of Denmark. It felt both strange and special being one of the only American tourists there, as confirmed by how confused staff members were when I showed my CDC card as proof of vaccination. Most places I went to didn't have many tourists at all.

When I was done at the museum, I headed to Nyhavn, the famous canal with brightly covered buildings that you see anytime you search anything about Copenhagen tourism. I figured it wouldn't be anything special, since I've seen it in photos twenty times at that point.

What happened next might be one of the most profound experiences of my life.

When I arrived, I felt an intense, out of body experience. The vibrant colors of the buildings, the beautiful Christmas lights draped at the markets in front of them. The emptiness of the street I was viewing them from, so free of other tourists that I felt like an explorer discovering a special place that no one had discovered before.

And suddenly, I found myself overwhelmed by this feeling, and couldn't help but start to cry.

Right in that moment, I felt everything that it took to get there. The anxieties of the day before, and the weeks leading up to it. The months and months of preparation to move to Europe, to be able to take trips like I was taking now. During all of that time, all of the endless tasks and logistics to move, I wasn't sure if it would be worth it. But as I wiped my tears away, I couldn't stop smiling, feeling happier than I had ever felt in my life. Because at that moment, I knew that it was.
label: personal_experience
note: sharimg Dublin travel experience

text:
Late-30s Couple Travel Inspiration
Hi All!

We are a couple in our late-30s and looking for travel inspiration. We don't want another resort vacation, so we're trying to expand our horizons. We have the last week of August and the first week of September booked off.

We have been researching destinations, but tend to get a bit overwhelmed when it comes to the logistics. I decided to look into companies like Flash Pack, G Adventures, and Intrepid, but the regimented itinerary puts us off slightly. We're also wary of "organized fun" (we've both spent way too long work in corporate jobs so dread the idea of being stuck in "tell us a fun fact about yourself" circles). It's not that we are anti-social, it's just that we are really looking for a trip where we focus on enjoying chatting and hanging out with each other, and less so with new people.

Our rough ideas/preferences:

\- We are travelling from Canada.

\- We enjoy "popping around" (walking somewhat aimlessly, finding fun knick-knacks, seeing cool buildings, and stopping in for a few drinks and some people watching). 

\- We like lively, but we don't want all-out party.

\- Beaches would be preferable, but not essential if there's an obvious pick that isn't beachy.

\- We're not adrenaline junkies in any capacity, but we also don't want to sit/lay down the entire time. The most 'adventurous' we're likely to get would be hiking or kayaking.

\- We'd love if it was more of an 'experience', and a chance for something different - whether it be cool history, awesome scenery, or great food.

\- We'd like to make sure we're being conscientious travellers. We don't want to knowingly or unwittingly participate in something fucked (drugged-up animals, etc.).

\- We are looking to get some much needed relaxation, as it's been a pretty stressful year, so we don't want a destination that requires a wall-to-wall itinerary, or a sequence of city breaks.

\- The U.S. is not an option (incl. Hawaii) and I'd prefer non-Europe.

My research so far has mostly led me to Thailand or Vietnam, but I'd love to hear other ideas. I'm hoping that there are some well-informed people on this sub who might be able to give us some inspiration, recommend websites that might help reduce the organizational complexities, or share some experiences of group tours for semi-social couples.
label: advice_seeking
